root.note: Most scholars take cervesia to be a Celtic word from Gaul that Latin borrowed. Others link it to Ceres, the goddess of grain, as Isidore of Seville already did.

history: When you order a cerveza, you may be using a word from before the Romans. Or perhaps not. Pliny knew cervesia as a drink of Gaul, and most scholars take the word for Celtic, perhaps linked to Irish coirm, ‘beer’. But Isidore of Seville connected it with Ceres, goddess of grain, and some modern writers defend that idea. So we mark it disputed. What is clear is that the word survives only in Iberia: Spanish cerveza, Portuguese cerveja, Catalan cervesa. Most of Europe took a Germanic word instead, as in French bière, Italian birra and English beer. Medieval French once had cervoise, but it is now obsolete.
historyEinfach: Cerveza means ‘beer’. The old Latin word was cervesia. Probably the Romans took it from the Celts in Gaul. Some people think it comes from Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain. Experts don't agree. Only Spain and Portugal kept this word. Most languages in Europe use a word like beer, birra or bière.

elsewhere.text: Portuguese is the close relative: only the Iberian languages kept this word.
French now says bière, but it once had cervoise, from the same Latin word as cerveza.
English beer is a Germanic word, unrelated to cerveza.
Italian also took the Germanic word.
German Bier is the source of the word most of Europe uses.
